claims.text: Fast cooling equiatomic NbMoTaW yields a largely single-phase microstructure with minimal precipitate content.
Post-solidification annealing of equiatomic NbMoTaW induces nanoscale precipitate formation.
The annealing-induced nanoscale precipitates are stable under high-temperature service conditions.
The distribution, size, coherency, and coarsening behavior of the precipitates govern the proposed response.
Nanoscale precipitates alter local elastic or stress fields.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by the precipitates increases the high-temperature yield strength of annealed NbMoTaW.
Precipitate-induced changes in local stress fields produce a distinct high-temperature thermoelastic anomaly.
Relative to the fast-cooled baseline, annealed samples will exhibit higher yield strength.
Relative to the fast-cooled baseline, annealed samples will exhibit nonlinear stress-strain behavior or modified elastic moduli.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure may coarsen the precipitates and diminish their strengthening and thermoelastic effects.
The proposed effects apply within the service-temperature range of refractory high-entropy alloys provided precipitate coarsening is controlled.
A controlled comparison between fast-cooled and annealed NbMoTaW specimens can test the precipitate-mediated hypothesis.

The hypothesis is falsified if annealed samples show neither a statistically significant yield-strength increase nor a distinct thermoelastic anomaly relative to the fast-cooled baseline, or if coarsening eliminates the microstructural difference.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis describes the annealing-induced precipitates as stable, while the uncertainty field states that their long-term stability at service temperatures is unknown and that coarsening may diminish their effects.
